description.summary: Qdrant is an open-source dedicated vector database and search engine for storing, filtering, and retrieving dense, sparse, named, and multi-vector representations.
description.description: Qdrant provides exact and HNSW-based vector search, structured payload filtering, dense-sparse hybrid retrieval, multi-stage queries, disk-backed storage options, quantization, and distributed sharding and replication. It is available for self-hosted deployments and as Qdrant Cloud. This record separates documented engine capabilities from configuration-, workload-, and deployment-dependent guarantees.

indexingConsiderations: Create payload indexes for fields used by production filters, preferably before ingesting data, so filtered HNSW construction can account for those fields.
Choose exact search, HNSW parameters, on-disk storage, and quantization only after measuring recall, latency, memory, and ingestion behavior on representative data.
Size shards and replicas for the expected cluster topology; self-hosted clusters require explicit planning for shard placement, movement, and rebalancing.
Treat named dense, sparse, and multi-vector spaces as separate retrieval representations with explicit dimensions, metrics, and lifecycle management.
retrievalConsiderations: Use payload filters together with appropriate payload indexes and test strict or combined filters against the chosen HNSW search configuration.
Tune dense-sparse fusion with a relevance evaluation set; RRF, weighted RRF, and distribution-based score fusion make different ranking assumptions.
Place fusion at the top-level query when a distributed collection requires results to be fused globally across shards.
Set read consistency, write consistency, and ordering options according to the required tradeoff among latency, availability, and concurrent-update consistency.

limitations: HNSW, on-disk indexing, and quantization introduce workload-specific tradeoffs among recall, latency, memory, storage, and indexing cost.
Strict or compound filters can reduce HNSW graph connectivity; payload-index design and search-method tuning remain necessary.
A self-hosted distributed deployment does not automatically rebalance existing shards when nodes are added or removed.
High availability requires replication and an appropriate number of voting nodes; a two-node cluster cannot retain a Raft majority when one node is unavailable.
Concurrent updates can diverge across replicas under default settings unless stronger read consistency, write consistency, or update ordering is selected.

Qdrant does not provide general multi-record ACID transactions comparable to a relational database; update durability and ordering guarantees are scoped to its point, WAL, shard, and cluster mechanisms.
usageGuidance: Record the Qdrant server and client versions because API behavior, storage migrations, and supported query features change across releases.
Build a representative relevance evaluation set before choosing HNSW, quantization, fusion, or multistage-query parameters.
Create snapshots and test restoration procedures even when replication is enabled.
Use payload indexes selectively for fields that participate in filters, faceting, ordering, or tenant partitioning.
Upgrade self-hosted clusters through supported intermediate versions when release notes document storage-format or migration constraints.

references.title: Qdrant Documentation: Hybrid and Multi-Stage Queries

claims.statement: Qdrant supports dense, sparse, named, and multi-vector representations and provides exact dense-vector search or approximate dense-vector search through HNSW.
claims.rationale: Official Qdrant documentation describes the supported vector representations and distinguishes exact search from HNSW-based approximate dense-vector retrieval.

claims.statement: Qdrant supports structured payload filtering and can augment HNSW construction with payload-index-aware edges to improve filtered vector search.

qualifiers.name: configurationScope
qualifiers.value: Payload indexes must be created for fields that should participate efficiently in filtered search

claims.rationale: The filtering and indexing documentation describes boolean, range, text, geo, nested, and related payload conditions, and explains payload-index-aware filtered HNSW behavior.

claims.statement: Qdrant's Query API supports dense-sparse hybrid and multi-stage retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, weighted RRF, and distribution-based score fusion.

qualifiers.name: versionScope
qualifiers.value: Hybrid Query API capabilities documented through Qdrant 1.18.2

claims.rationale: The official hybrid-query documentation provides dense and sparse prefetch examples and documents RRF, weighted RRF, DBSF, nested prefetches, and multistage queries.

claims.statement: Qdrant supports distributed collections with sharding and replication, while read consistency, write consistency, and update ordering can be configured to change the balance among availability, throughput, and consistency.

qualifiers.name: deploymentScope
qualifiers.value: Distributed mode; operational automation differs between self-hosted Qdrant and Qdrant Cloud

claims.rationale: The distributed-deployment documentation describes Raft topology consensus, shards, replicas, read consistency, write consistency factors, ordering, and deployment-specific shard operations.

claims.statement: Qdrant supports in-memory or memory-mapped vector storage, on-disk HNSW, and multiple quantization methods that trade memory and storage usage against recall and search behavior.

qualifiers.name: versionScope
qualifiers.value: Qdrant 1.18.2, including TurboQuant introduced in the 1.18 release line

claims.rationale: Official storage and quantization documentation describes RAM, memmap, on-disk HNSW, scalar, binary, product, and TurboQuant configurations and their tradeoffs.

evidence.summary: Official Qdrant sources document dense, sparse, named, and multi-vector representations together with exact and HNSW dense-vector search.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can model Qdrant as a dedicated database supporting Flat, HNSW, and hybrid sparse-dense retrieval.

sourceFragments.locator: Overview sections: retrieval workflow, architecture, and client-server interfaces
Vectors sections: Dense Vectors, Sparse Vectors, Named Vectors, and MultiVectors
Indexing sections: vector index and HNSW configuration

limitations: Project documentation establishes supported capabilities but is not an independent performance benchmark.
Recall and latency depend on vector distribution, hardware, collection size, filters, and search parameters.

evidence.summary: Qdrant documents structured payload filters and recommends creating payload indexes before ingestion so filtered HNSW can use payload-aware graph edges.
evidence.interpretation: Qdrant supports pre-filtered retrieval, but efficient and well-connected filtered search depends on payload-index and HNSW design.

sourceFragments.locator: Indexing section: HNSW with payload indexes and filtered-search graph edges
Filtering sections: clauses, match, range, full text, geo, nested, and payload-index guidance

limitations: Strict combinations of filters can still fragment the effective HNSW search space and require tuning.
Creating payload indexes consumes memory and indexing resources, so indexing every payload field is not advised.

evidence.summary: The Qdrant Query API documentation combines dense and sparse prefetches and documents RRF, weighted RRF, DBSF, nested prefetches, and multistage rescoring.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM hybrid-search profile can include sparse-dense fusion, reciprocal-rank fusion, weighted fusion, and score normalization.

sourceFragments.locator: Vectors sections: Sparse Vectors and Named Vectors
Hybrid Queries sections: Query API, Hybrid Search, RRF, DBSF, and Multi-Stage Queries

limitations: No fusion strategy is universally best; quality must be measured on a representative relevance set.
In distributed collections, query nesting and the placement of fusion affect whether ranking is shard-local or global.

evidence.summary: Qdrant's distributed-deployment documentation describes sharding, replicas, Raft topology consensus, configurable read consistency, write consistency factors, and update ordering.
evidence.interpretation: Qdrant has high horizontal-scaling capability, but resilience and consistency depend on node count, replica placement, and selected request and collection settings.

sourceFragments.locator: Distributed Deployment sections: Sharding, Replication, Node Failure Recovery, and Consistency Guarantees

limitations: Collection topology operations require a Raft majority; a two-node cluster loses that majority if either node is unavailable.
Self-hosted shard rebalancing and some replica operations require manual administration.

evidence.summary: Qdrant documents in-memory and memmap storage, on-disk HNSW, and scalar, binary, product, and TurboQuant compression methods.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark disk-backed indexing and multiple quantization approaches while retaining explicit recall-memory-latency tradeoffs.

Quantization sections: Scalar, Binary, Product, and TurboQuant
Release v1.18.2 and the 1.18 release-line context

limitations: Compression and on-disk configurations must be benchmarked with the actual embedding model and storage hardware.
Quantization can reduce recall, and rescoring or oversampling can increase latency or I/O.
